title: Why the US midterms are a rare foreign policy election
author: LToremark
description:
Why the US midterms are a rare foreign policy election Expert comment LToremark 15 October 2026

US voters are linking economic concerns to the Trump administration’s foreign policy choices. This is bad news for Republicans.

Foreign policy rarely decides US elections. Conventional wisdom is that voters know little, and care less, about international affairs. Instead, they are driven by pocketbook issues, like the price of gas and groceries. As James Carville, an adviser to Bill Clinton, once observed: ‘it’s the economy, stupid’.  But this year, the economy is foreign policy.

There are two important exceptions to the rule that US voters don’t care about foreign policy – and they both apply this year. One, voters care about foreign affairs when an administration’s choices directly affect their daily lives. Two, voters care about what foreign policy choices reveal about a president’s competence as commander-in-chief. 

The upcoming midterms could therefore be a rare foreign policy election – of a kind not seen since 2006 when a backlash to George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq war handed Republicans a ‘thumping’ defeat. 

With voters now feeling the pain of yet another war in the Middle East and Trump’s tariffs, history could repeat itself. The president seems aware of this risk, sending mixed signals about whether the elections will shape his handling of the war in Iran and striking a deal on diesel exports with Russia to ease the pain at the pump for voters.

But perhaps the bigger question is what Trump does after the midterms, the last major electoral check on his presidency. 

War on the ballot

Become a corporate member

Give your organization access to trusted geopolitical analysis, policy insight and expert networks to help leaders anticipate risk, navigate uncertainty and make informed decisions.

War has always been the clearest example of when foreign policy directly affects the daily lives of voters.

But this is not always reflected in polls about the importance of individual issues – and this year is no different. Voters cite economic issues as the key drivers of their vote. In a recent survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, pluralities of voters across the political spectrum cite inflation and the cost of living as most important to their vote (37 per cent overall). By contrast, only 2 per cent single out the war in Iran as the most important issue, possibly due to the relatively low number of US casualties.

But that does not mean it is not having an impact. Voters are linking the pain in their pocketbooks with the foreign policy choices of this administration. According to a recent survey by the Institute for Global Affairs, 81 per cent of Americans say the war in Iran has increased the cost of living. The Chicago Council survey puts the number even higher, at 86 per cent.

And then there are the trade wars. According to the Chicago Council survey, 81 per cent of respondents say tariffs have been bad for the cost of living. It is unsurprising, therefore, that 75 per cent of Americans say tariffs will be important to their midterm vote, according to a survey by the Cato Institute.

Importantly, these findings cannot be written off as partisanship. Across a whole range of issues, support for Trump’s policies lags well behind his overall approval rating – which continues to hover around a historic low of 37 per cent. This suggests voters are not just instinctively opposing anything the president does but that large numbers of Americans, including many who otherwise support him, do not like his policy choices.

Affordability concerns will still dominate these elections. But large numbers of Americans blame the administration’s foreign policy choices for the perilous state of their household finances. And that’s bad news for Republicans.

From a strong leader to a reckless one

The second exception is when prominent foreign policy missteps tarnish the image of the sitting president in ways that cause voters to take note.

For example, how the Biden administration handled the 2021 US withdrawal from Afghanistan severely damaged perceptions of Joe Biden. His approval rating dropped almost overnight and never recovered.

In 2024, Trump was able to turn this into an advantage on the campaign trail by presenting himself as a strong leader who would stand up against America’s adversaries – and with a commitment to peace.

Today, Trump’s reputation is suffering from both his inability to resolve foreign policy challenges he inherited and the abandonment of his pledge to avoid entangling the US in costly conflicts overseas.

In a CNN/SSRS survey, just 29 per cent of US adults said they approved of Trump’s handling of foreign affairs, down from 42 per cent shortly after he returned to office. Only one in four respondents believed he had a clear strategy for handling Tehran, down from 40 per cent in the immediate aftermath of the outbreak of the war. 

These dynamics also appear to be feeding into broader perceptions of Trump’s leadership. In a YouGov survey fielded at the outset of the war, 56 per cent of respondents said the word ‘reckless’ applied ‘a lot’ to Trump – up five points from a year ago – while the proportion who described him as a ‘strong leader’ dropped four percentage points. 

To what degree will foreign policy shape the results – and how will Trump respond?

Related work

What the US midterms could mean for Trump’s power

Republicans were already likely to fare poorly. The midterms are traditionally seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent president, and with Trump’s overall approval ratings at a near-record low, history is not on his side.

Even though foreign policy may not dominate any given race, it is likely to matter at the margins. And in a tight race, that could make all the difference.

In some swing states Republican candidates are distancing themselves from the president’s policies. In Michigan, Senate nominee Mike Rogers has said the war ‘needs to end, and end quickly’, to provide relief for American families. In Iowa, meanwhile, Senate nominee Ashley Hinson similarly said that Iowans ‘shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran’. 

Trump’s diesel deal with Russia indicates some sensitivity to the electoral risks of high gas prices. But achieving this by accommodating Vladimir Putin – rather than an embargo on US diesel exports, for example – has only highlighted another foreign policy weakness: Trump’s inability to end the war in Ukraine.

But will an electoral rebuke result in more foreign policy restraint? Perhaps the most important question is not the degree to which foreign policy will shape the results, but how the president will respond. 

And here, history offers a warning. After his 2006 midterm defeat, President Bush did not change course. Instead, he defied the mandate voters had given by escalating an unpopular war in the Middle East.

President Trump recently pledged not to attack Iran before the midterms, having previously expressed a desire to help his party in the elections. Whether he too will try to end the war through a dramatic escalation once the ballots are counted remains to be seen. 

But he would not be the first president to double down on an unpopular policy once unshackled from electoral constraints. The ‘lame duck’ phase of Trump’s presidency may therefore prove even more disruptive on the international stage.

title: Responding to US sanctions on the International Criminal Court
author: sfarrell.drupal@chathamhouse.org
description:
Responding to US sanctions on the International Criminal Court Expert comment sfarrell.drupa… 15 October 2026

The US decision to extend sanctions has upped the ante in its campaign against the ICC. The Court’s supporters must decide how to respond, perhaps now it is time to put all options on the table.

On 9 October 2026, the US designated the International Criminal Court under Executive Order 14203, extending its existing sanctions package on individual ICC officials to the entity itself as a whole.

The US imposed asset freezes on any property owned by the Court and prohibited all transactions by US individuals or entities involving the ICC.

The US has allowed certain limited exceptions to this general prohibition, to allow for the ongoing detention of some awaiting trial, the payment of pensions, the use of IT software and social media and a 180-day ‘wind down’, allowing certain otherwise prohibited transactions until April 2027.

These sanctions were introduced by the US in what Secretary of State Marco Rubio called an ongoing campaign to ‘dismantle the ICC brick by brick’.

‘For decades, Republicans and Democrats alike rejected the idea that the International Criminal Court had the power to prosecute American citizens, military service members, or political leaders. America never joined the court. We don’t need it. And we don’t want it,’ Rubio said in a statement.

‘We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defense, to rein in the court. If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer,’ he added.

The ICC called the sanctions ‘an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.’

Those countries that have signed up to the ICC – the ‘State Parties’  – now have to decide how to respond, through diplomacy; support or the ‘nuclear option’.

The impact

An asset freeze essentially prevents making any economic resources available directly or indirectly to the ICC.  They must be observed by all US persons and green card holders, wherever they are in the world, all US companies and any person in the US. 

They also apply to any transactions or data routed through the United States. In reality, this can often limit (at best) and prevent (at worst) nearly all financial transactions of a designated person.

As such, if left unchecked, the US sanctions could severely hamper the day-to-day operations of the ICC.  The General Licence operates to provide a wind down period, but at most provides a stay of execution and the potential for diplomatic efforts to reverse or mitigate the impact.

The Court itself noted that whilst it endeavours to continue functioning as normal, international cooperation is imperative as the Court’s fate also rests in ‘the hands of the States that created it’. 

So far, foreign ministers of the UK and others have issued a Joint Statement affirming their unwavering support for the ICC. The EU has also said that it stands ready ‘to take all necessary measures to ensure the Court continues to operate effectively and fulfils its indispensable mandate’. 

Below are recommendations on how the UK government may best respond to the ICC designation in coalition with other State Parties.

Diplomatic Engagement 

State Parties should open the dialogue as necessary to address the US concerns regarding the authority of the ICC. 

The 180-day Maintenance General Licence, marked as a show of good faith, intends to achieve just that. It provides State Parties the chance for diplomatic engagement.  The ICC’s Assembly of States Parties in December will provide an opportunity to review and align the response of the State Parties to the US.

Practical Support: Preparing for the Worst

In parallel to diplomatic efforts, State Parties can start to consider what practical assistance they can provide in the event that diplomatic efforts are unsuccessful or that companies start de-risking sooner rather than later and start to withdraw services before the expiry of the US General Licences that could impact – as no doubt the US intends – the ongoing investigations and operations of the Court.

As such, whilst the US General Licence might allow for a 180-day ‘wind down’ of the provision of crucial goods and services, companies caught by US sanctions may simply decide to stop working with the Court at any time.

That means the State Parties need a comprehensive plan to support the Court, covering everything from provision of IT to support on banking and payment routes, and everything in between.

Blocking Statute: the Nuclear Option

Some State Parties – in particular the UK and EU Member States – may have the option of turning to the ‘Blocking Statute’.

This has been dubbed the ‘nuclear option’ by Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen. It would essentially prohibit any natural or legal person from complying with US sanctions.

But Blocking Statutes have only been deployed vary rarely in the past, primarily targeting US extra-territorial over-reach where it has imposed sanctions against countries like Cuba and Iran, and required those outside of US jurisdiction to comply with them.

However, even this nuclear option’ is not without its limitations. First, it won’t be available to all State Parties without new primary legislation. Second, even where the legislation is in place, it is not clear that the US measures would fall squarely within the legislation which is designed to protect ‘trading interests’ against extra-territorial measures. An argument could certainly be made, but it could face challenge if ever relied upon.

Third, it only applies to those caught by the relevant jurisdiction. In the UK and EU, for example, the prohibition on complying with the US sanctions would only have to be observed by UK/EU nationals, UK/EU companies or those operating in the UK or EU.

Finally, it essentially puts domestic companies between a rock and a hard place – fail to comply with US sanctions or fail to comply with the UK/EU ‘Blocking Statute’.

State Parties with this potential option have not deployed it despite the US targeting of judges and Court staff; perhaps now the US has upped the ante in its campaign against the Court, it is time for its supporters to put all options on the table.

title: Accounting for cross-country income differences: Two decades of progress
author: David Lagakos, Todd Schoellman
description: Development accounting is a simple tool with potentially powerful insights. It asks whether the measured differences in inputs between developing and developed countries can account for the gap in GDP per worker. Twenty years ago, Francesco Caselli famously argued that the best estimate was “no”. This column revisits that conclusion in light of two decades of intensive research. The authors show that inputs account for a much higher share than previously thought – between 55% and 70%, as opposed to 30% before. An expanded measure of human capital that incorporates education quality and work experience drives much of this result.

title: Tokenised finance: Towards better markets?
author: Benoit Nguyen, Imène Rahmouni-Rousseau
description: Tokenised finance has moved from the margins of crypto markets to the centre of the policy agenda. Central banks, regulators, and market participants are debating how far it could reshape the issuance, trading, and settlement of securities, including what this would mean for financial markets and monetary policy. This column argues that while tokenisation offers considerable promise — including near-instant settlement, round-the-clock operations, and higher velocity of liquidity and collateral — the transition to a tokenised world will not be frictionless. The coexistence of 24/7 on-chain systems with traditional off-chain infrastructures could create new challenges for market functioning and monetary policy implementation.

title: Small is beautiful 2050: Europe’s digital economy as a mesh, not a hub

description: In response to digital dependence, Europe has decided to think bigger. This includes AI gigafactories, tripling data centre capacity, and searching for domestic champions. However, this column argues that the destination for 2050 should be different. For the first time since the railway age, small, open AI models that run close to the data are making it possible for network technologies to distribute economic power rather than concentrate it. Europe’s dense network of small firms, regions, and languages puts it in a strong position to reap the benefits, provided today’s rules on switching, procurement, computing, and diffusion are designed with a mesh in mind rather than a hub.

title: The Swiss–Japanese immigration puzzle

description: Anti-migration politics are advancing across the rich world at very different levels of foreign population. Japan has a foreign-resident share just above 3%, while Switzerland’s foreign-born share is near 30%. Yet both have recently experienced a surge in nationalist politics centred on migration, suggesting that the scale of immigration alone cannot explain the backlash. This column argues that neither economic nor demographic pressures provide a sufficient explanation. Evidence from the Swiss vote of June 2026 and Japan’s elections in 2025–26 points to a generational dimension: support for migration restriction is strong among the old but also younger voters, while attitudes toward immigration appear less changed than its political salience.

title: War has returned to Tigray. This time it may not stay in Ethiopia
author: LToremark
description:
War has returned to Tigray. This time it may not stay in Ethiopia Expert comment LToremark 1 October 2026

As fighting escalates in Tigray and neighbouring areas, there are fears that Ethiopia’s internal instability could spill over into the wider Horn of Africa region.

Conflict returned to Ethiopia’s northern region of Tigray on 23 September, as the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) forces stormed three national airports in Tigray. In what the TPLF claimed was defensive combat, ground offensives were also expanded along Tigray’s southern and eastern borders with the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions. The TPLF and its allies captured parts of Afar but lost several key areas in southern Tigray, including Alamata town.

Ethiopia’s federal government forces and the allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) are now advancing towards Mekelle, the capital of Tigray. Meanwhile, reports of drone strikes in Addis Ababa and on government-controlled airbases alters the nature of the war.

Although Tigray has seen conflict before, this time there is a risk that hostilities could extend into Eritrea and Sudan.

The slow creep towards renewed conflict

Related work

Ethiopia needs more than an election to calm internal and regional conflict

The risk of renewed hostilities in Tigray had been clear for some time, given the steady decline in relations between the federal government and the TPLF. The failure to build on the Pretoria Agreement – the ceasefire deal that brought an end to the war in 2022 – was largely the result of a continued zero-sum approach by both sides, as well as weak implementation and oversight.

The agreement effectively unravelled in May, when the TPLF reinstated a pre-war legislative council, with its chairman Debretsion Gebremichael named regional president. This spelled the end of the Tigray Interim Regional Administration (TIRA) – a key outcome negotiated under Pretoria. The removal of interim president, General Tadesse Werede, formerly head of the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF), followed the ouster of his predecessor Getachew Reda in late 2024.

The TPLF views the recent escalation as a return to full-scale war. To an extent, they have been pushed towards a response. There is continued containment of Tigray; a lack of implementation of the Pretoria Agreement or any dispute resolution mechanism; the absence of incentives for its leadership to return to the federal fold; a weakening of TPLF legitimacy in the region; and recent drone attacks by the government in the region.

But unlike in the 2020–22 war, the federal government has been more cautious and calculated in its actions as well as public messaging. The government frames the TPLF as a rogue administration that is colluding with internal opposition insurgencies and external actors to threaten Ethiopia’s territorial integrity and its own survival.

The key question now is whether the government will seek to contain the conflict within Tigray and other parts of northern Ethiopia, or whether it will consider it necessary to pursue bolder options. One such option could be targeting Eritrea, which it believes to be supporting anti-government movements – something Eritrea has repeatedly denied. In a message assigning culpability to its northern neighbour, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea and expelled Eritrean diplomats.

Now, much will depend on how the conflict evolves.

Internal division in Tigray and a new opposition alliance

The TPLF’s control over Tigrayan society has weakened significantly. Since the war ended in 2022, it has faced protests over crippling economic conditions, growing competition from rival parties and defections by leading members. In recent months, Tigrayan authorities have turned to forcibly recruiting young men into the defence forces and have cracked down on freedom of speech. For the people of Tigray, an already difficult humanitarian situation now looks set to worsen. 

There is deep division within TPLF too. Following the start of the military offensive, there have been reports of senior TPLF officials being arrested or defecting to Addis Ababa.

Days before the fighting resumed, the TPLF and six other regional armed opposition groups – including Amhara’s Fano movement and the Oromia region’s Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) – announced a coalition called the Alliance for Survival. Their common goal is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his Prosperity Party from power and install a transitional government.

But it is not immediately clear that this uneasy tactical alliance – among groups with unresolved tensions and very different visions for Ethiopia – will result in functional cooperation. Senior leaders of Fano have publicly opposed the alliance; while a recently divided OLA may struggle with justification to its support base. There are also historical grievances between some of these groups. The TPLF have accused Fano and the Eritrean forces of grave human rights violations in Tigray four years ago, while Fano and OLA have been bitter and at times violent enemies.

Risk of regional spillover

Related work

De-escalation is needed to prevent Ethiopia and Eritrea from going to war

Opposition to the Ethiopian government also comes from beyond the country’s borders. Tsimdo is a transnational alliance which reportedly links the TPLF, the Eritrean government and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).

The TPLF is silently allied with its former foe, Eritrea, with supply lines chiefly secured through Tigray’s northern border. But the Eritrean government’s priority is to keep war away from its own territory, and its alleged support for opposition groups increases the risk of further regional escalation – especially with Ethiopia eyeing control over Eritrea’s Red Sea port of Assab.

Meanwhile, the conflicts in Ethiopia and Sudan have also become more intertwined. The Ethiopian government has accused the SAF of backing the TPLF – which they have denied – and is increasingly unsettled by the reported presence of Tigrayan fighters alongside the SAF in eastern Sudan. It fears that the SAF, in collaboration with Eritrea, could reinforce the TPLF from across the Sudanese border – including near strategic sites like the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.

Sudan, in turn, has accused Ethiopia of providing support for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudan People’s Liberation-North (SPLM-N), including training, supplies and use of Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia’s close ally, the UAE, is also accused of supporting the RSF – although it refutes such allegations. Ethiopia’s calculus is seemingly to create a buffer on its border with Sudan. However, direct dialogue and de-escalation with the SAF would go further than retaliatory exchanges and mutual accusations of interference.

Limited options for de-escalation  

The mediation landscape is very different from 2022. Members of the international community have called out the TPLF for their escalatory actions and urged a return to African Union (AU)-led talks. The Ethiopian government has so far controlled the narrative around this conflict, briefing foreign governments about the likely escalation ahead of the UN General Assembly.

The Pretoria Agreement did not produce the broader political settlement needed for durable peace and no longer seems tenable for either side. The TPLF has repeatedly discredited the only existing mediation effort under the AU. Hardening regional rivalries and the lack of US or wider Western interest to fully support the AU with the resources and leverage needed to create a viable platform, makes a sustainable resolution to this conflict seem a long way off.

Given these conditions, the conflict is likely to continue for a while. However, the danger of diplomatic inaction is that a protracted war in Tigray is likely to spill over beyond Ethiopia, into Eritrea and further into Sudan. Policymakers must find a way to take collective action to avert such a dangerous regional escalation.

title: How the insurance industry can help society adapt to climate change
author: LToremark
description:
How the insurance industry can help society adapt to climate change Expert comment LToremark 1 October 2026

As climate change threatens to make homes uninsurable, the insurance industry is often the bearer of bad news. But its understanding of future risks can be used to help society adapt to a warming world.

There are increasingly frequent headlines about how climate change is affecting insurance coverage and affordability: homeowners in areas prone to wildfires, hurricanes or flooding discovering that their existing policies cannot be renewed, or that cover has become unaffordable or vanished altogether. The word often attached to these stories is a stark one: uninsurability.

Beyond the headlines, banks worry about what declining cover means for the value of properties securing long-term mortgages. In turn, regulators worry about the systemic consequences if large numbers of properties lose value at once. Mayors worry about gaps in coverage impacting long-term investment in their cities. Governments, meanwhile, are becoming more interventionist as people are being priced out of protection, stepping in to keep cover flowing.

They are right to worry. But framing the problem as insurance failure misdiagnoses what is going wrong – and lets everyone else off the hook.

Uninsurability is a symptom of deeper problems 

Want to hear more on the path to a secure energy transition?

Join us at our climate and energy summit, where policymakers and industry leaders tackle the toughest questions on climate and energy security.

The term uninsurability implies that the issue lies within the insurance industry. But it is almost always a symptom of deeper problems – of which climate change is the most important, but far from the only one.

California is perhaps the most famous example of climate-driven market failure. While wildfire risk has undoubtedly risen, the retreat of insurance was as much a consequence of political choices to suppress premiums as of climate change. When the true cost of risk collides with an artificial cap on what may be charged for it, cover does not just become expensive – it becomes uneconomic to offer at all. Climate change did not break the market on its own; the market failed because society was unwilling to pay the true price of the risk it faced.

The pattern is repeated elsewhere. Yes, rising premiums reflect climate change. But they also reflect dysfunctional planning systems that permit construction in areas prone to climate hazards and decades of chronic underinvestment in risk reduction and resilience. Insurers are, in effect, the messengers: rising prices are among the first clear signals that risks have become intolerable. And shooting the messenger is always a tempting option.

The dangers of blaming insurers

The narrative that insurance is failing carries real reputational and regulatory danger for the insurance industry. As rising premiums and thinning cover drag on property values, societies will look to place blame and insurers risk becoming scapegoats for a collective failure they did not cause. Governments may respond with more intervention, tighter constraints on pricing and more pressure to write cover at a loss.

This narrative also creates danger in society at large. Insurers have built a uniquely sophisticated architecture to understand and price risk. That architecture is now increasingly signalling a stark truth: as climate change intensifies, historical decisions about where and how to build are rapidly becoming too costly – or too challenging – to maintain. When the plight of homeowners in California and elsewhere is only viewed as a failure of insurance, we miss the opportunity to have a vital public conversation not only about making today’s society resilient, but also about what structural changes and trade-offs are required for societies to thrive in a rapidly changing climate. 

Prominent industry voices sounding the alarm on insurability can be helpful if the result is greater government action on emissions and adaptation. But it is not enough on its own. As climate impacts intensify, insurance will find itself dragged into uncomfortable political arguments about who bears the cost of loss and damage, which places are worth defending and which will have to be abandoned. This is unavoidable; insurance will shape these outcomes by determining what gets cover, who is compensated and who pays. An industry that has cast itself only as the bearer of bad news risks becoming viewed as part of the problem.

Where insurance can – and should – do more 

All this obscures how much agency insurance has. Arguably no other industry is better placed to help societies adapt to climate change. Insurers have the data and models to anticipate how risks are evolving – exactly the intelligence governments and developers need to decide where to build and what to adapt. Risk-based premiums, so often cast as the problem, are among the most powerful adaptation signals we have. And insurers’ risk-advisory teams can help design the defences, retrofits and hardened infrastructure that keep places insurable in the first place.

Related work

Europe’s summer of fires: Burnham must centre climate adaptation in policies

This is not only about defending markets and preserving insurability – it is a genuine growth opportunity that also addresses a pressing societal need. A recent report from the UK Government Office for Science estimated cumulative global adaptation spending of £3.5 trillion over the next decade, with insurance highlighted among the sectors positioned to benefit. Other estimates of the market potential for adaptation goods and services are even higher. It is likely to be one of the defining market opportunities of the next 20 years.

The imperative is to get off the back foot: stop being the messenger and start being a solution. There are already signals of change. Capitalizing on this momentum means three things. One, being far clearer about what is needed from national and local governments on adaptation – not vague calls for ‘better planning’, but concrete asks tied to the risks insurers can see coming. Two, putting the industry’s modelling and advisory expertise to work on adaptation, visibly and at scale. Three, making peace with increased government intervention. Historically, the industry has eyed public schemes and public–private partnerships with suspicion, concerned that they will crowd out private insurance. But the use of these schemes will grow as concerns about insurability mount. Insurers should instead help shape them so they reduce risk rather than subsidise its accumulation, and support adaptation rather than undermine it through blunted price signals.

What governments should do

Climate adaptation is rapidly gaining momentum but is too often focused on technical solutions to flood and heat, not the economic and social architecture required to make adaptation a reality. Governments need to build the mechanisms for insurance to engage on adaptation early and at scale. At the national level, this could include establishing country platforms to coordinate and finance adaptation strategies. Similar mechanisms could be developed at the city level. Above all, governments must start having the conversations everyone would rather avoid: about where societies should adapt and where they should retreat – and they must involve insurers in these discussions. 

The retreat of insurance from the climate front line is real and frightening. But it is also an opportunity. Read as a failure of the insurance industry, it will misdirect blame, encourage clumsy market interventions and delay adaptation. Read as information – and met by an industry willing to move from warning to action – it could instead prompt the urgent work and hard choices that a warming world demands. That choice, for now, is still ours.

author: Mátyás Farkas, Zoltan Jakab, Jesper Lindé
description: Nominal interest rates increased significantly in the US and euro area following the post-pandemic inflation surge, yet economic activity and labour markets remained resilient. This column finds that accounting for policy expectations implies a larger increase in the natural rate of interest, r*, than standard approaches suggest. In the US, r* increased by around two percentage points and around 1.5 to 2 percentage points in the euro area. These increases are largely explained by changes in convenience yields. Thus, monetary policy stances were considerably less restrictive than commonly believed and this helps explain the soft landing in economic activity.

title: Changes in the health and longevity of the elderly in the US
author: Liran Einav, Amy Finkelstein
description: Spending on public pensions through Social Security and on elderly healthcare through Medicare accounted for over one-third of federal expenditures in the US by 2024. This column explores how improvements in elderly health and life expectancy affected the relative finances of Social Security and Medicare. The elderly are not only living longer but also are in better health, so expected lifetime Medicare spending per elderly individual has grown much slower than expected lifetime Social Security spending. The authors analyse the forces that affect the optimal allocation of a given public budget across these two social insurance programmes.

title: Chasing far-right does not pay for the centre-right parties: Evidence from Germany’s 2025 election
author: Nina Nikiforova
description: Establishment parties are often urged to win voters over from populist parties by shifting their policy positions towards them. Based on the 2025 German federal election, this column simulates what would happen when the centre-right CDU changes its policies and the populist radical-right AfD responds. If the AfD stood still, a modest shift to the right would win the CDU a fifth of AfD voters, but the AfD would respond by moving further right, undoing the CDU’s gain. This strategy can thus leave the CDU worse off while pulling politics further to the right. Once the AfD's response is anticipated, moving right is no longer optimal for the CDU.

title: Fiscal consolidation: Temporary costs versus lasting scars
author: Luiz de Mello, Joao Tovar Jalles
description: Public debt is at or near record highs across the OECD, increasing the pressure on governments to restore fiscal sustainability over time. This column draws on new cross-country evidence showing that the output costs of fiscal consolidation are modest and short-lived on average, and that lasting scars are hard to detect. But averages conceal a critical asymmetry: consolidations launched in high-debt environments are markedly more contractionary, and in more than half of the episodes in the sample the debt ratio was still higher three years after consolidation. Initial fiscal conditions matter more for outcomes than the choice between spending cuts and tax increases.

title: Never let a good crisis go to waste: Term limits and banking reforms
author: Orkun Saka, Yuemei Ji, Clement Minaudier
description: Financial crises routinely trigger sweeping overhauls of financial regulation, but whose interests do these reforms serve? Using data on financial policies in 88 democracies between 1973 and 2015, this column shows that leaders facing a binding term limit roll back financial liberalisation roughly three times more than leaders who can run again – but only in the wake of a financial crisis. The reforms they enact tend to favour incumbent banks over the general public. The effect is concentrated in countries where revolving doors between politics and finance are common, brings post-government career benefits to policymakers, but leads to no gains in banking stability.

title: US midterms polls: Are Democrats winning or is Trump losing?
author: thilton.drupal
description:
US midterms polls: Are Democrats winning or is Trump losing? Expert comment thilton.drupal 28 September 2026

Polls suggest Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives as American voters are dissatisfied with President Trump and his policies.

Americans go to the polls on 3 November to elect a third of the US Senate and all the House of Representatives. 

The Republicans currently have majorities in both chambers of Congress. But their prospects of retaining this control look increasingly dire.

The Republicans’ chances have been dragged down by President Donald Trump’s near-record low public approval rating and voter dissatisfaction with his handling of the Iran war and the economy, among other things. Democrats appear poised to take advantage, with most pundits suggesting they will retake control of at least the House of Representatives. 

But the race is not over yet. In the end, the key factor will likely be turnout, which is historically lower in midterms than presidential elections. Whichever party better mobilizes their voters to turn up on election day will ultimately determine the outcome. 

Democrats are strong favourites

At this point, this election is the Democratic Party’s to lose. 

Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in the 435-seat House of Representatives. To control the House, which gives a party the ability to name chairmen of committees and set the legislative agenda, the Democrats will need to win at least 218 seats. They currently have 212 seats.

Due to polarization and redistricting, most seats are highly unlikely to change party. Election analysts estimate that only around 21 House seats are close contests or ‘toss-ups’. Still, most pundits forecast Democrats winning between 220 and 230 seats overall – a relatively comfortable majority. 

Senate more challenging

The Democrats face a more difficult challenge recapturing the Senate. Republicans now hold 53 of the 100 seats. Given that the vice-president can cast a tie-breaking vote in the Senate, the Democrats will need to win four seats (and not lose any they currently hold) to gain control of the Senate. 

They are likely to pick up a Senate seat in North Carolina, where the state’s former two-term Democratic governor, Roy Cooper, has a significant lead in the polls. Then things get harder for the Democrats. 

They need to win contests in three other states currently represented by Republicans. Current polling suggests their best chances are in Alaska, Maine, Ohio, Texas and Iowa. 

Public opinion surveys show all five races to be toss-ups. But the Democrats also need to defend a Michigan seat that is considered a toss-up, where the incumbent Democratic senator is retiring in a state Trump won in 2024. 

If the national tide swings heavily in the Democrats’ favour, they could gain control of the Senate. But that is less likely than their chances of winning the House.  

Public dissatisfaction 

Public opinion has been generally downcast ahead of the election. Two-thirds of those surveyed in May think the country is headed in the wrong direction. A July survey found only about a quarter of the public think the economy is doing well, with concerns over the cost of healthcare, food, housing and gasoline. Most recently, a majority said going to war with Iran was the wrong decision.

More registered voters think the Democrats would do better than the Republicans in dealing with gas prices, the economy, and foreign policy. 

Democrats also have a 6 to 14 point advantage in nationwide polls of voter intentions known as the ‘generic ballot.’ This question measures party popularity by asking a selection of registered voters nationwide which party’s candidate they intend to vote for, without naming specific candidates. Historically, the generic ballot is a key indicator; the Democrat lead suggests a majority on election day.

Moreover, in the last five midterm elections, there has been a change in control of at least one chamber of Congress. And only four times in the last 164 years has the president’s party gained seats in a House of Representatives midterm election.

Voter turnout in midterm elections is usually relatively low compared with presidential elections: averaging less than 50 per cent compared to roughly 60 per cent. Voter enthusiasm will therefore be a big factor in maximizing turnout. Polls suggest Democrats are more motivated to vote: 79 per cent of Democrats said they are extremely motivated to vote, compared with 69 per cent of Republicans. 

The Trump factor

Looming over all of this is voter opinion about President Trump, the ever-present force in current American politics. 

The most recent Reuters/Ipsos poll has Trump’s approval rating at 32 per cent, a new low for him, with a disapproval rate of 66 per cent. 

Other recent polls have shown Trump’s approval rating ranging from the mid-30s to low-40s; a recent YouGov poll put it at 37 per cent. But a recent poll by the American Research Group, conducted 16–20 September, showed the president with just a 29 per cent approval rating – the first time it has dropped below 30 per cent.

Historically, presidential approval matters in congressional elections. For context, Trump’s ratings are significantly lower than either President Bill Clinton’s in 1994, when the Democrats lost 54 House seats and 8 Senate seats, or President Barack Obama’s in 2010, when Democrats lost 63 House seats and 7 Senate seats. 

Majorities disapprove of how Trump is handling all major issues. And a plurality of registered voters, including a majority of independents who make up about a third of the electorate, say their vote in the congressional election is ‘mostly against Trump’. 

The potential impact of Trump’s low approval on the November outcome has led Charlie Cook, a leading political analyst, to observe not a ‘blue wave’ but the effects of a ‘red undertow.’ Either way, Democrats appear well-positioned to take advantage of disapproval with Trump to make congressional gains.

Caveats

But as with any forecast, there are caveats. While Democrats may be more motivated to vote overall, polling shows that 83 per cent of Republicans who strongly support President Trump claim they are absolutely certain to vote in November. Moreover, Republicans have the advantage of much larger finances as they try to mobilize their voters. 

The electorate is also more polarized between Republicans and Democrats than at any time in recent history. And congressional gerrymandering means that there is a relatively small margin of error for Democrats. 

So, despite the various factors that point to a Democratic victory in November, the election could still tighten. 

Not over yet

Ultimately, voters decide elections, not pollsters. And recent election polling has repeatedly underestimated Republican support, as Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris learned to their dismay. 

Historically, American voter intentions are unlikely to change this close to election day. But US elections are also notorious for October surprises: the deepening financial crisis in 2008 and developments in the Hillary Clinton email probe in 2016 are just two examples. 

The World Today

Related work

What will happen if Trump rejects the midterm results?

It is also possible that 4 November will dawn without a clear victor. The president’s previous challenging of election results and processes, for example with regards to postal votes, could mean potential disputed outcomes and court challenges. This could delay final results for days or weeks, further undermining the reputation of American democracy.  

Polls suggest the Democrats are poised to win the US House and possibly the Senate. But, as the American baseball player Yogi Berra once said: ‘It ain’t over till it’s over.’

title: Brazil’s presidential election is more than just another polarized contest
author: jon.wallace
description:
Brazil’s presidential election is more than just another polarized contest Expert comment jon.wallace 28 September 2026

A Bolsonaro victory would mean Trump-aligned governments dominate South America.

The first round of Brazil’s presidential election is scheduled for 4 October, with 13 candidates competing to occupy the Brazilian presidential palace, Planalto.  

For now, the contest is dominated by two men. Only a few percentage points (depending on the poll) separate 80-year-old President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party (PT) – running for his fourth term – and 45-year-old Flávio Bolsonaro of the right-wing Liberal Party (PL). 

Flávio is the son of the man Lula defeated in 2022, former president Jair Bolsonaro (2019–23), sometimes referred to as the ‘Trump of the tropics’. Lula squeaked out a narrow victory in the 2022 contest, of 50.9 to 49.1 percent in the second round, after public opinion surveys had seriously undercounted the support of his right-wing rival. Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving time for plotting a coup, after his supporters rioted in Brasilia in 2023 in an effort to overturn the 2022 results. 

This year’s contest is more than a familial grudge match. For one, it looks a lot like recent presidential elections in the region. In June, elections in both Peru and Colombia went to a second round. Each resulted in a narrow victory for conservative candidates who, like the Bolsonaros, are aligned with the regional diplomatic agenda of US President Donald Trump.  

Another tight contest now looms in Brazil, the most populous country and largest democracy in Latin America, the tenth largest economy in the world, and for decades an international champion of the Global South, through blocs like BRICS.  

Both Lula and the younger Bolsonaro face high levels of voter rejection. More than 54 per cent of Brazilian voters disapprove of Flavio according to one poll. Lula does little better in the same survey, with 52 per cent against the president running for a fourth term.  

The issues

Brazilian voters are divided over a number of issues relating to Brazil’s political system and its place in the world.

According to a Pew survey conducted in Brazil in early 2026, only 37 per cent of Brazilian voters were satisfied with their democracy, down from 66 per cent in 2013. And Brazilians are ideologically split on favourable views of China versus the US.  

57 per cent of Brazilians who identify as leftist have favourable views of China, compared to 40 per cent of those on the right. Those opinions flip on attitudes towards the US: 58 per cent of self-identified right-leaning voters have favourable views of the US, while only 30 per cent on the other side of the ideological spectrum do.  

Division on these issues indicates that this election could have major implications for the direction of Brazil’s foreign policy, its global influence, and the PT foreign policy agenda since 2003. 

Brazil’s situation is not unique. Distrust in democratic electoral systems has increased around the world – a sentiment that outsider political entrepreneurs have exploited. Their ability to do so stems from political polarization, discontent with the political class – and the simple fact that casting a ballot and accepting the aggregate macro tabulations of all voters requires a certain commitment of faith. As political tribes have become more separated and disconnected from alternative views and media, it becomes easier to feed on distrust, suspicion and resentment. 

According to a recent Chatham House/ Convergent Opinion survey, distrust in the electoral system is greater among those who voted for then-president Jair Bolsonaro in 2022 than those who voted for Lula that year. 

Only 45 per cent of 2022 Bolsonaro voters expressed very much or some confidence that elections would be free from political interference this year, compared to 78 per cent of 2022 Lula voters. That is concerning, but not necessarily surprising. Jair Bolsonaro cast doubt on the integrity of Brazil’s electoral system before the 2022 elections. (Flávio has promised to respect this year’s election outcome. But he has also vowed to grant amnesties to those who took part in the 2023 riots).

Fuelling this division is an escalating diplomatic row with the administration of US President Donald Trump. In July, the US imposed new 25 per cent tariffs on some Brazilian goods. The same month, the Brazilian government denied visas to two US envoys, accusing them of planning to meddle in elections – a charge the US State Department called a ‘baseless lie’. 

The diplomatic dispute has escalated further, with the White House revoking the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US, and Lula’s office accusing the US of ‘a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons’. In his speech at the UN General Assembly on 22 September, Lula warned against foreign interference in the election.

The potential foreign policy about-face

A Bolsonaro victory this year would create another friendly South American government for the Trump administration, adding to the White House’s growing list of aligned leaders (either for transactional or ideological reasons) in Colombia, Venezuela, Paraguay, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Dominican Republic, and Ecuador. 

Related work

Trump’s ‘Shield of the Americas’ coalition is destined to fail

Indeed, a Bolsonaro government would probably adhere to Trump’s approach on various issues, including a more martial approach to narcotics trafficking and transnational criminal networks operating in or from Brazil. It will likely see Brazil joining Trump’s Shield of the Americas initiative.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency would also bring a U-turn to PT-focused foreign policy agendas. It would trigger, if not a pulling out, then a significantly reduced role in the BRICS group, which Trump has criticized for ‘anti-American policies’. And Brazil might well draw back from other global forums, such as the UN, the G20, and COP where Brasilia has staked its claim as a representative of the Global South.

In reality, under the PT, Brazil’s track record in supporting multilateralism has been spotty. Often it has been partisan in defending human rights and democracy even in its own neighbourhood. 

Equally, it is not clear that a new Bolsonaro government would represent a triumph for Trump’s so-called ‘Donroe Doctrine’, which seeks to establish American supremacy in the Western Hemisphere. 

While a Bolsonaro-led Brazil would return Brasilia to his father’s anti-woke cultural battles, it would not necessarily fall into line with the Trump White House, particularly on trade. Bolsonaro distanced himself from Trump’s heavy tariffs. And, as was true for his father and neighbour Argentine president Javier Milei – who both had campaigned on reducing Chinese influence – a new Bolsonaro administration would balk at reducing trade with China, Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009. China, though, may seek to reduce its Brazilian imports, if Bolsonaro strays too far in challenging Beijing.  

Regardless, Brazilians face a stark choice in October. Brazil’s commitment to international law and multilateralism hangs in the balance, as does the Global South’s voice in the global order.

title: Can Gulf Arab countries help break the deadlock over Trump’s Gaza peace plan?
author: LToremark
description:
Can Gulf Arab countries help break the deadlock over Trump’s Gaza peace plan? Expert comment LToremark 21 September 2026

Gulf Arab states increasingly view Israel as the main obstacle to progress on the peace plan – and may hope for an opening after Israel’s October elections.

Almost a year after US President Donald Trump unveiled his 20-point peace plan for Gaza, which was adopted by both Israel and Hamas and paved the way for the release of all Israeli hostages, the peace process appears to have hit a wall.

The two sides remain fundamentally divided over the sequencing of demilitarization and Israeli withdrawal. So far, Hamas has refused to give up its heavy weapons unless Israel halts all military operations and withdraws its forces from the parts of Gaza it currently controls – approximately 60 per cent of the strip – while Israel says it will not withdraw until Hamas disarms. 

Although President Trump continues to argue that the situation in Gaza is under control, his envoy Jared Kushner, who recently visited Israel, and the director-general of his Board of Peace, Nikolay Mladenov, have so far been unable to launch the second phase of the process. 

Related work

The Iran war has left Gaza neglected

In September, Kushner acknowledged that the task of demilitarizing Gaza was proving far more difficult than initially expected: ‘We are starting to understand the scope of the militarization of Gaza. It is beyond your comprehension’. In August, he had told Fox News that he expected Hamas to begin handing over its weapons in ‘as few as 30 days’. 

Meanwhile, the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains critical according to an August report by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) – and there is little hope for reconstruction given the current stalemate. According to the OCHA report, 58 per cent of Gaza’s population is facing ‘severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or access to essential services and non-food items’, while a severely strained health system and lack of medical supplies could put lifesaving services at risk. 

Arab Gulf countries like UAE (which is also a member of the Board of Peace) are key providers of humanitarian aid to Gaza. In fact, UAE aid accounts for 46 per cent of global assistance. But what is their position on the current stalemate in Gaza and could they help find a way to break the deadlock?

In August, eight Arab and Islamic countries – Saudi Arabia, UAE, Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia, Turkey and Qatar – condemned Israel’s unwillingness to proceed with the implementation of Trump’s plan for Gaza, saying its stance threatens international efforts to end the war. 

In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of these countries denounced Israel’s stated opposition to a roadmap for completing Trump’s broader Gaza plan, which was endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2803. The group also called for Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups to disarm; an Israeli military withdrawal; the deployment of an international stabilization force; the transfer of administrative authority to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza; and the reconstruction of Gaza.

In May, it was reported that the UAE had contributed $100 million for training of new Gaza police force – an important feature that will help provide security in post-war Gaza. However, Israeli officials reportedly barred the already vetted new recruits from leaving the strip for training in Cairo, and for now it is unclear when permission to leave and return to Gaza will be granted – if at all.

Although the UAE and other Arab members of the Board of Peace did not comment on this report, it is clear that their frustration with the Israeli government over Gaza and the West Bank is mounting. In August, the inaugural ‘Emirates loves Palestine’ event was held in Dubai, celebrating the connection between the UAE and the Palestinian people, while a delegation from a UAE future leaders programme were sent to Egypt to learn about – and take part in – UAE efforts to provide humanitarian aid to Gaza.

Indeed, the UAE is particularly important in this context as it is one of the signatories of the Abraham Accords and one of Israel’s closest partners in the Gulf and the Arab world. But other Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have also sharpened their condemnation of recent radical statements by Israeli officials on the forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza, as well as increasing settler violence in the West Bank. Trump, meanwhile, has insisted that a controversial nuclear deal signed with Saudi Arabia this summer hinges on Saudi normalization with Israel. But despite US pressure, it seems the Saudis will not divert significantly from their demand to establish a clear path for Palestinian statehood.

Related work

Israel’s general election will be like no other before

Due to the Iran war and its fallout, Gulf Arab states are more preoccupied with their own domestic security and economic challenges than at any point in recent memory. And with only weeks to go until Israel’s pivotal October elections, they also retain a measure of hope that a change of government could open the way to more constructive engagement. 

Leading opposition candidates in Israel have been critical of Netanyahu’s policies on both Gaza and the West Bank. Many of them believe that Israel needs to involve the Arab states, and in particular Saudi Arabia, in future dealings with the Palestinians. A new Israeli government could also prove significantly tougher on settler violence in the West Bank and more flexible on alternative Palestinian governance in Gaza to unseat Hamas. 

However, if the current governing coalition remains in power, more drastic and radical steps might follow. This could include construction in the E1 strategic perimeter, which would drive a wedge through the West Bank and undermine prospects of a future Palestinian state, as well as a possible escalation in Gaza.

For now, Gulf states are focusing on two key diplomatic instruments in their response to the ongoing stalemate in Gaza. One is humanitarian assistance, the other is pointed condemnations of Israel, which is increasingly perceived in Arab capitals as the primary obstacle to the implementation of Trump’s peace plan.

At present, it seems unlikely that Gulf states will change tactics. Even less likely that they will withdraw support for Trump’s peace plan and the Board of Peace, or press for urgent, extraordinary measures, such as sanctions on Israel or an intervention by Trump himself. But this calculus may well be revised in the aftermath of the Israeli elections, depending on the outcome. It will also remain contingent on the broader strategic environment in the Gulf, not least the risk of renewed hostilities. 

Until something breaks the stalemate, the population of Gaza will continue to be caught between Hamas and the Israeli government – both waiting for the other to make the first move.

title: Water has emerged as a key issue for Arizona voters ahead of US midterms – governments should take note
author: LToremark
description:
Water has emerged as a key issue for Arizona voters ahead of US midterms – governments should take note Expert comment LToremark 12 October 2026

The case of Arizona shows that governments must stop treating water as merely an environmental issue.

US President Donald Trump may dismiss the threat posed by climate change, but its consequences are becoming harder for US voters to ignore. Take Arizona, for example, where water has emerged as an unusually prominent issue ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Recent polling found that long-term water supplies was the top concern for Arizona voters, after federal cuts to the state’s water supply from the drought-stricken Colorado River. Water has consequently become a prominent issue in Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs’ re-election campaign, with opponents accusing her of mismanaging Arizona’s water supply in an effort to undermine her bid for a second term.

Water is no longer just an environmental issue 

Arizona is an extreme example, but the underlying dynamic is much broader.
Water is fundamental not only to drinking and sanitation, but to almost every aspect of an economy. In Arizona, it underpins agriculture and urban development, while also supporting industries and amenities that can seem particularly incongruous in a desert environment, such as golf courses. Now a new source of demand is emerging: data centres, driven by the rapid growth of cloud computing and artificial intelligence. The Phoenix metropolitan area ranks second in North America for proposed data-centre development, raising questions about the impact of these energy- and water-intensive facilities on already stretched water supply – an emerging big issue in the midterms. 

Related work

AI water usage requires governments to rethink their approach to water

Arizona’s water predicament is being intensified by a changing climate. Already one of the hottest and driest states in the US, Arizona is experiencing rising temperatures that increase evaporation and water demand, while intensifying drought. This is also putting further pressure on the Colorado River, which supplies more than a third of Arizona’s population, while groundwater reserves are being depleted in parts of the state. 

But climate change is only part of the story. Water crises are rarely caused by climate alone. Decades of groundwater over-abstraction, inefficient agricultural practices, pollution, poorly maintained infrastructure and allocations based on historical assumptions can turn a drought into a systemic crisis.

And this is not only an American problem. Cape Town’s 2018 ‘Day Zero’ crisis demonstrated how quickly drought, population growth and rising demand can turn water scarcity into a political emergency. Tehran offers another warning, where drought and declining rainfall have combined with groundwater depletion, and decades of water-management decisions to produce a systemic crisis. European cities like Barcelona, Madrid, Athens, Rome and even London have all faced emergency water restrictions in recent years as drought intensifies.

Companies are paying attention too. The World Economic Forum’s global risk assessments have repeatedly identified water supply shortages among the risks facing economies and businesses. Water shortages can disrupt agricultural supply chains, manufacturing, electricity generation, construction, real estate and technology infrastructure.

Water security is increasingly also about economic and political security.

When water crosses borders, scarcity becomes political

The political challenge becomes even harder when water crosses administrative boundaries.

Arizona’s position within the Colorado River system is governed by a complex web of agreements and legal arrangements, some dating back more than a century. The 1968 legislation authorizing the Central Arizona Project, for example, gave its Colorado River deliveries junior priority, meaning Arizona would face reductions before California in specified shortage circumstances.

As the river comes under increasing pressure, these historical arrangements have become politically consequential. The latest federal proposals for managing the Colorado River envisage substantial reductions in water deliveries to the three lower-basin states – Arizona, California and Nevada – with Arizona facing particularly significant cuts: 27 per cent this year and reductions could nearly double after 2028 if the drought worsens.

The underlying problem is therefore not simply that there is less water. It is that agreements and institutions designed for a different hydrological reality are being used to distribute a resource whose availability is becoming more uncertain.

Related work

The Climate Briefing: Contested waters in international politics

The same dynamic exists internationally. For example, Ethiopia’s plans to develop three new hydropower projects on the Blue Nile have reignited tensions with Egypt, which remains concerned about how upstream water is stored and managed, particularly during drought. The long-running dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam illustrates how greater hydrological variability and more frequent drought can put existing water-sharing arrangements under growing strain.

Water can therefore become a geopolitical issue even when that is not the intention. When a river or reservoir crosses political boundaries, a reduction in supply also becomes a question of who gets less.

Policymakers must move beyond crisis management 

Arizona offers a particularly vivid warning, not only to the US government but to governments around the world, because water has become a political issue before it has run out. 

The first step is to stop treating water primarily as an environmental issue. It is increasingly central to decisions on infrastructure, industry, agriculture, housing and public health, and, where water crosses borders, to foreign and security policy.

Water availability needs to be considered much earlier in decisions about where and how economies grow. If a region is chronically water-stressed, governments – as well as regional, state and local authorities – should ask whether new housing, agriculture or industrial development can be supported by available water supplies over the long term.

Technology will have an important role. Wastewater recycling, leakage reduction, precision irrigation, improved groundwater monitoring, more efficient cooling systems and, in some coastal locations, desalination can help expand the options available.

But technology alone cannot change the realities of water availability. The harder question is therefore what societies choose to build – and where.

This is also where nature-based solutions come in. Restoring wetlands can improve water storage, filter pollutants and reduce flood risk. Protecting watersheds can support groundwater recharge and improve downstream water quality. Restoring degraded soils and changing agricultural practices can improve water retention and reduce irrigation requirements.

These measures can deliver several benefits simultaneously – water security, biodiversity, flood protection, carbon storage and resilience to extreme heat – often at lower cost than purely engineered alternatives.

Finally, governments need to integrate water, land use, energy, agriculture and economic planning, both domestically and with neighbouring countries that share water sources, using realistic projections of future water availability rather than historical averages. Water-sharing arrangements should also be revisited as conditions change, before scarcity turns technical disagreements into political crises.

The emergence of water as a political issue in Arizona is striking in a political environment dominated by concerns over the cost of living, immigration and the Iran war. The fact that it has become a leading concern among voters in one of America’s fastest-growing states shows that water security is crossing an important threshold: from an environmental concern that governments can defer, to a question about what kind of future is physically possible.

title: Sánchez’s gamble: This ‘all-in’ election will have international impact
author: jon.wallace
description:
Sánchez’s gamble: This ‘all-in’ election will have international impact Expert comment jon.wallace 5 October 2026

Announcing the election, Sánchez set himself in opposition to President Trump and Javier Milei as well as Spain’s populist right. Much will depend on the prime minister’s ability to rally a fragmented left.

The decision by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election is a risky move, but he will have felt he had little choice. His decision fires the starting gun on a year of vital and polarized elections across Europe.

The announcement is not entirely unexpected. Spain was required to hold an election by August 2027 anyway. And Sánchez’s multiparty coalition has looked fragile since it formed in July 2023: it has not passed a full budget since. 

In January, the government approved a decree that regularized the status of 500,000 undocumented migrants and asylum seekers – a move unusual among EU countries generally committed to tightening migration restrictions. In July, the Spanish enclave of Ceuta was overwhelmed by a surge of tens of thousands of migrants, leading to criticism of government policy from within Spain and abroad, including US President Donald Trump. 

This month, a new issue has arisen, as protests grow over housing affordability. The protests prompted the government to introduce emergency legislation, only to see the bill rejected by Spain’s Parliament late last week. This gave Sánchez his opening to call a general election, arguing that ‘to do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people’. 

What are Sánchez’s chances?

Sánchez is a proven survivor and faced similar difficulties in 2023. But calling an election now is a gamble. The summer’s crises have given his political opponents plenty to work with, and trouble assails the prime minister and his party, the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), from every side. 

The opposition on the right will use the January decree and images of the Ceuta crisis to rally their vote and criticize the government’s competence. The left will point out the housing crisis has deteriorated under Sánchez. Then there are the corruption scandals that plague the prime minister. Some of his closest political allies are embroiled in the Koldo case – an investigation into corruption in health procurement contracts during the COVID-19 pandemic. In a separate case, the prime minister’s own wife has been charged with embezzlement and corruption.

To survive, Sánchez will use the same playbook that worked for him in 2023, where he characterized the contest as a choice between ‘Sanchismo’ (his brand of social democrat politics) or a ‘backward-looking’ far right. 

Related work

The Ceuta border crisis heaps pressure on Spain’s Sánchez government – and European unity

His hope will be that opposition to the PP right wing opposition party – and far right Vox party in particular – will mobilize left wing voters in a highly polarized contest. Vox leader Santiago Abascal regularly speaks of a ‘migrant invasion’ and used Sanchez’s January decree to call for ‘Repatriations, deportations and remigration’. 

Notably, Sánchez’s speech on the steps of La Moncloa (the Spanish prime minister’s residence) put international talking points at the centre of his pitch, contrasting his positions with the those of the right, and particularly US President Donald Trump and Argentinian President Javier Milei:

‘We have strived to build a better world for our fellow citizens and for the rest of humanity,’ he said, ‘supporting Ukraine, the European Union, and the United Nations in their darkest moments. Denouncing genocidal regimes when others remained silent.

‘Fighting tyrants, techno-oligarchs, and speculators who want to destroy the future of our sons and daughters to enlarge their pockets. Doubling our aid to international cooperation while others boasted of cutting it with their chainsaw or on that military altar of 5 per cent of GDP.’

Spain’s voting system

50 days of intense campaigning and negotiation between parties will now follow. These negotiations matter because of Spain’s electoral system. 

Spain uses the D’Hondt method in provincial constituencies, which punishes parties polling in low single figures. Small parties can survive by running together on a joint list, but past attempts have had mixed results. 

Sumar is the largest of these groupings. Despite having no leader, it has launched ‘Frente Amplio’ (the Broad Front) to try to pull support together. Much will depend on the firebrand MP Gabriel Rufián. He is seen as a potential unifier of the fragmented parties to the left of PSOE. But he is not a Sumar figure, and internal politics and personalities have a habit of wrecking electoral pacts in Spain. Podemos, PSOE’s coalition partner, joined Sumar’s list in 2023 but broke away within months.

For Sánchez, what happens to his left matters more than ever. His pitch therefore needs to be binary. Expect him to use Trump, Milei and Flávio Bolsonaro (ahead in Brazil’s presidential race after the first round) as bogeymen to focus minds even before the ballots are printed.

On the right, the Partido Popular (PP) will likely approach a ‘Ming Vase strategy’ of trying to just get through the next 50 days without any major mishaps. It is not clear that this can work. Questions about what a coalition with Vox would look like will follow their leader Alberto Feijóo. His inability to respond adequately to such questions in 2023 likely cost him victory. 

Spain’s vote will now be the first in a series of crucial European elections. France chooses a new president in spring 2027. Italy, Poland, Finland and Greece are due to vote before the year is out. Many of these contests will look like Spain’s, with some seeing fragile coalitions on the left facing a confident and surging right. 

The results will matter well beyond domestic politics. For instance, as the US continues to demand the continent do more for its own defence, disruptive elections will make it harder to make progress on a more coherent joint European approach to security. This campaign will be closely followed across the continent – and from across the Atlantic – as politicians seek to perfect their pitch in ever more polarized times.

title: Nepal’s floods put the global loss and damage system to the test
author: jon.wallace
description:
Nepal’s floods put the global loss and damage system to the test Expert comment jon.wallace 5 October 2026

Nepal’s recovery from August’s catastrophic glacial flood will test the efficiency of the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. It will also resurface questions about the responsibilities of the greatest carbon emitters.

On 26 August 2026, a glacial disaster high in the Himalayas sent a wall of meltwater and debris tearing through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Rasuwa region at speeds of nearly 188 km per hour. The flood has claimed over 1400 lives, with thousands still missing.  

Nepal is experiencing the consequences of a warming cryosphere, with accelerated glacier melt that could undermine the long-term security of a water source on which millions of people depend.  

The country only contributes around 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet its people are on the front lines of climate change impacts, as glacial retreat reshapes the Himalayan landscape. Early estimates of the cost of reconstruction are $4 to 5 billion, around a tenth of Nepal’s GDP. 

Nepal’s government has appealed to the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) for help. But that can only provide a fraction of the funds required. As a result, Nepal has raised the responsibility of the world’s largest carbon emitters and will bring the issue to the forefront of November’s COP31 climate summit in Turkey.

In this respect, Nepal’s recovery will stress-test bigger questions: How far is it possible to establish whether climate change was a contributing factor to a disaster? Can international climate finance mechanisms deliver urgent help to countries facing imminent, irreparable losses? And what more should the world’s greatest emitters be doing to help countries like Nepal?

The Fund faces a credibility test

Since the FRLD was established at COP27 in 2022, demand for financial support has far exceeded available funding. As of March 2026, 27 countries pledged $822.06 million, of which only around half was received. The Fund made $342 million available in its first round, dwarfed by requests of close to $2.8 billion for losses and damages worldwide.

The Fund faces disbursement delays from unreliable capital flows and institutional bottlenecks, due to unfulfilled voluntary commitments and approval processes within the World Bank. Nepal’s access is also constrained by complex, multi-tiered federal approval processes and lengthy procurement procedures.

At present, there is no rapid-access pathway for countries to apply for FRLD funding outside scheduled application windows. Questions also remain about how the Fund will assess the role of climate change in causing particular disasters, and how such assessments might influence funding decisions.

Nepal has emerged as an early test of how the Fund will respond. Kathmandu has requested $20 million – a modest sum compared to the scale of economic damage. Yet the request is significant for what it reveals about the Fund’s ability to respond in practice: Can the Fund move resources quickly and predictably enough to provide support when it is most needed?

Scientific attribution 

Nepal’s catastrophe puts attribution front and centre: how can it be established whether climate change was a contributing factor to a disaster, rather than the sole cause? If it is found to be a contributing factor, when is that sufficient to establish harm? And is it possible to apportion responsibility for global warming to greenhouse gas emissions by certain countries?

Nepal is relying on a recent flood study in its claim to the Fund, attributing several cascading climate factors to the onset of this catastrophe. This should make Nepal’s case for loss and damage straightforward. The harm is tangible, the science exists, and the FRLD was built for this scenario. But a fund capped at $20 million per project is facing a disaster impact estimated in billions. That may push Nepal to look past the Fund’s limits to the countries whose emissions may have contributed to these harms. 

In July 2025, the International Court of Justice’s Advisory Opinion on Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change offered a real, if partial, legal scaffolding to claims that states suffering climate-related harm may seek address, a development relevant to Nepal’s application to the FRLD. On establishing harm, the Court accepted that climate science can be relied upon to link specific disasters to climate change. A ‘sufficiently direct and certain’ standard was set to accommodate the complexity of determining causality in climate events. 

Responding to losses and damages 

Speaking at the UN General Assembly last Friday, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah argued that the FRLD and other mechanisms remain ‘grossly inadequate’ for countries like his, which contributed little to warming of the Himalayan climate. This followed calls by his foreign minister for major emitters to work together to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal. 

By seeking support from major emitters across developed and developing countries, Nepal is challenging established understandings of climate responsibility and raising difficult questions about who should bear the costs of climate-related losses.
